alignment.note: ἐκ νεκρῶν / ܡܢ ܡܝܬܐ / a mortuis

All three render the aorist/perfect 'they rise from the dead'; the Syriac places the verb ܕܩܡܘ before the prepositional phrase ܡܢ ܡܝܬܐ, inverting the Greek and Latin order in which the verb (ἀναστῶσιν / resurrexerint) follows 'from the dead'. The divergence is purely sequential.

Greek γαμοῦσιν and Latin nubent express 'they marry' with a single verb; the Peshitta uses the periphrastic idiom ܢܣܒܝܢ ܢܫܐ ('they take women/wives'), an explicit object construction characteristic of Syriac, which makes the male subject of the active clause overt.

Where Greek and Latin repeat a single negative conjunction (οὔτε / neque), the Peshitta employs the compound ܐܦ ܠܐ ('and not, neither'), a normal Syriac coordinating negation rather than a substantive difference in sense.

Greek γαμίζονται and Latin nubentur use a single passive verb 'are given in marriage'; the Peshitta paraphrases with ܢܫܐ ܗܘܝܢ ܠܓܒܪܐ ('women become [given] to men'), shifting to a feminine subject and supplying explicit nouns, an idiomatic Syriac expansion that clarifies the implicit gender contrast of the Greek active/passive pair.
ἀλλά / ܐܠܐ / sed; the duplicated Greek token (ἀλλ᾽ with transliteration) is a single conjunction.

Greek uses an articular attributive phrase οἱ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς ('the [ones] in the heavens') with the plural οὐρανοῖς; Latin renders a bare prepositional phrase in cælis, while the Peshitta compresses the whole into a single relative form ܕܒܫܡܝܐ ('who/that are in heaven'). The Greek article οἱ has no separate equivalent in Latin or Syriac, and the heaven-noun is plural in Greek/Latin but morphologically singular-collective in Syriac.
